evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.4.5: magnae tibi levātiōnī solitus sit esse
terms.comment: “It is a relief to me”: mihi levātiōnī est, with the double dative. With a genitive, what is eased: levātiōnem habēre aegritūdinum, to bring relief from grief (Cic. Tusc. 1.119, Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive: the person in the accusative, the trouble in the ablative
evidence: Cic. Att. 4.7.1: quae mē sollicitum … valdē levāvit
terms.comment: “I’m relieved” is the passive, levor, or the active with the letter or news as subject. It comes from levis, light, with a short e; lēvō, with a long e, is “make smooth”. To breathe again after a fright is respīrāre (see phew!).

evidence: Cic. Att. 12.43.1 (Lewis & Short): mihi illam rem fore levāmentō
Traupman 157: levāmentō esse, to be a relief
terms.comment: Something that brings relief, often in the double dative levāmentō esse.

phrases.latin: quae mē sollicitum dē Quīntō nostrō, puerō optimō, valdē levāvit
phrases.english: (your letter,) which was a great relief to me, anxious as I was about our Quintus, the best of boys

phrases.latin: nōn enim dubitō quīn magnae tibi levātiōnī solitus sit esse cotīdiānus congressus et sermō
phrases.english: for I don’t doubt that your daily meetings and talks with him used to be a great relief to you

sources: Lewis & Short: levatio · Lewis & Short: levo · Lewis & Short: levamentum
